articles.title: I’m in my late 60s and in a situationship with a man I really like. I want more but I’m scared of losing him
articles.summary: Don’t be afraid to speak your desires aloud, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith. These are pretty normal, humble things to want. I’m in my late 60s, divorced three years ago.
body: It’s been three months so far, the attraction was instant and strong and felt very promising. We see each other on weekends, which he has stated works for him (partly because he lives an hour away). I’ve told him that I would like to spend more time together and, because of his response, I decided I’d ease off and see what happens. I know he likes me, we get on well and I also know he’s not seeing anyone else. The contact we have in between is sporadic and it’s usually me that initiates it. If he does, it’s very casual. Bottom line – I feel like I’m getting crumbs.

The problem is I’m scared of losing him if I state more definitely what I need. It’s difficult to meet men at my age and, while I have a full and active life, I also crave the intimacy that can only be obtained in a relationship.
Eleanor says: I feel bad for our wants, constantly told they’re overwhelming for other people and pre-emptively ushered from the room.
“They’ll run away if they know what I want” is premised on the idea that your desires are so scary, so pressuring, that even learning about them might be too much for someone.
points: Don’t be afraid to speak your desires aloud, writes advice columnist Eleanor Gordon-Smith.
These are pretty normal, humble things to want.

articles.title: Gen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’
articles.summary: As Americans use apps like DoorDash and Uber Eats more habitually, they confront the guilt of paying extra fees for convenience. When it comes to food, Caroline Bauldree does not like to “deprive” herself of anything. She does not like to cook either, so that means a lot of food deliveries.
body: Bauldree got into the habit of near-daily DoorDashing back in college. “I could order whatever food from whatever restaurant and it showed up at my door – that’s the dream,” she said. “But then I just feel like crap about myself because I’m like, ‘wow, I’m a lazy piece of shit.’ Nine times out of 10, I feel bad about myself.”

There is a term for that post-order clarity: delivery guilt. The pandemic turned food delivery apps such as DoorDash, Uber Eats and Grubhub, once only popular in major cities, into a full-fledged national lifestyle. One Purdue study found that two-thirds of consumers used a food-ordering app at least once in 2024; another recent survey from the marketing company FinanceBuzz in partnership with Bank of America found that 57% of Americans get takeout or delivery weekly or more. Gen Z is more likely to feed the habit, clocking in an average of five orders a month – roughly double the monthly orders made by Boomers.

articles.title: Sedimentary rocks: why pét nat and cloudy wines are on the rise
articles.summary: There’s something refreshing about unfiltered or unfined wines. We filter through a selection … Centuries ago, Geoffrey Chaucer observed that “ther is no newe gyse that it nas old”.
body: So why choose a cloudy or unfiltered wine? “There’s texture, there’s fleshiness, there’s rounded fruit,” says Zainab Majerikova, head of wine for the Ottolenghi group, where the three house wines are unfiltered and cloudy natural numbers. “We think this makes them more moreish and a better fit for food with big, complex flavours,” says Majerikova.

I always get the sense that longer contact with lees (those dead yeast cells) makes cloudy wine more food-like; it might be a drink, but there’s a crunchiness to it. For the full effect of its flavours and weight on the palate, Majerikova recommends shaking a bottle of cloudy wine before opening to mix the sediment with the liquid. Either way, she says, cloudiness “brings soul, vibrancy and complexity” to wines for old-fashioned fun.
Trouble Cloudy Organic Rosé £12 Ocado, 12.5%. A slightly savoury, very drinkable take on a southern French rosé – bring on an Indian summer.
Alma 4 Phos Pét Nat £12 Tesco, 12.5%. Food-versatile pét nat Argentinian chardonnay from the Uco Valley, lightly sparkling and textural.

articles.title: Bottega Veneta Took Over the Guggenheim for Taryn Simon’s Big Night
articles.summary: Bottega Veneta gathered friends of the house at the Guggenheim to experience Father Country I Do Love You, multidisciplinary artist Taryn Simon’s monumental, decade-long undertaking, presented against the backdrop of the nation’s 250th birthday.
body: “It’s like a birth,” Simon said, describing the whirlwind of finally presenting the project. “I’m in a daze.” With a procession of admirers approaching her all evening, fresh from exploring the works and eager to share their impressions, there was hardly a second for her to catch her breath. Simon’s summation of it all? “There’s lots of blood. And exhaustion. Amazement, blood, and exhaustion.” As if on cue, novelist Salman Rushdie swept her into a long hug, followed by performance artist Marina Abramović.

The show marks both the first monographic exhibition by a photography-based artist in the museum’s rotunda and the largest debut of new work ever staged at the Guggenheim. Across 42 multipart artworks, which Simon calls “chapters,” she follows the real life of an unnamed federal agent, tracing the consequences of his actions and inactions through photographs, text, videos, and sculptures. “Oh my God! It’s just breathtaking,” exclaimed Julianne Moore in response to the exhibit. “I’m such a huge fan of Taryn’s. She’s an extraordinary artist, and what she manages to do in this show… she physicalizes a feeling, and does it in terms of personal relationships and lived lives.”

articles.title: You Can Now Join a WhatsApp Call Without an Account
articles.summary: The worst thing about your favorite chat app is trying to get your friends and family to use it. WhatsApp may be the most popular messaging platform in the world, but in the United States, it is hardly universally adopted. On the contrary, you'll find plenty of people who don't use it at all.
body: That's now changing. Meta, WhatsApp's parent company, announced "guest calling" on Wednesday. Now, any WhatsApp user can invite any non-WhatsApp user to a call, even if the recipient doesn't have an account. These calls still get the same core perks as traditional WhatsApp calls, Meta says: They're free and end-to-end encrypted, so you won't be compromising on your privacy by calling a non-WhatsApp user this way.

Non-WhatsApp users are still limited. Meta says these users always need a call host's approval to join. If you're a non-WhatsApp user, you'll find yourself in a waiting room until the call host lets you in. Meta also says that you can be kicked off the call at any time, and you won't be able to see other callers' phone numbers. You won't be able to send messages or add other users to the call. You are purely a participant.
points: The worst thing about your favorite chat app is trying to get your friends and family to use it.

articles.title: Meghan Markle Makes Her First UK Public Outing—With a Down-to-Earth New Look
articles.summary: Meghan Markle’s latest “official” engagement look is a far cry from her 2017 debut. This afternoon, the Duchess arrived in Nottingham wearing a burgundy double-face cashmere coat and matching knit from Joseph with Jennifer Chamandi heels.
body: Back in August, British Vogue drew up a handy shopping list of the British brands we might expect to see Meghan Markle wearing on her return to the United Kingdom. Judging by her recent appearances, however, she needed no such guidance.

Photographed today visiting The Community Recording Studio in Nottingham—where she and Harry made their first royal appearance after announcing their engagement in 2017—Meghan opted for a polished take on autumnal dressing in a burgundy double-face cashmere coat and matching knit from Joseph, paired with Jennifer Chamandi heels.

The British high street, it seems, is proving a reliable source for Meghan’s evolving wardrobe. Just yesterday, the Duchess was spotted in London wearing a blazer and jeans from Marks & Spencer, having stepped out earlier in the week in Boden trousers for dinner with Malala Yousafzai.

articles.title: Two Prada Gowns, One Big Cause: Inside Selena Gomez’s Rare Impact Fund Benefit
articles.summary: The fourth annual Rare Impact Fund Benefit included the presentation of the inaugural Katherine Short Legacy Award, named for the late daughter of Gomez's Only Murders in the Building costar, Martin Short.
body: Selena Gomez knows how to make an entrance—and a statement. On Wednesday night, the pop star and Rare Beauty founder arrived at the historic Hollywood Palladium in a custom crimson-hued Prada gown to host the fourth annual Rare Impact Fund Benefit. Gomez welcomed a record 500 guests for an evening where beauty came with a bigger purpose: raising funds and awareness for youth mental health issues.

Since launching Rare Beauty in 2020, Gomez has built a brand around boosting self-acceptance. That philosophy extends beyond the makeup bag through the Rare Impact Fund, which works to expand access to vital services and reduce the stigma around mental health conditions. The Fund, which aims to mobilize $100 million in contributions and receives 1 percent of Rare Beauty sales, has so far raised more than $30 million.

articles.title: Cher Talks Being a Style Icon (”It’s Fabulous!”) and Remembers Bob Mackie
articles.summary: The enduring icon—who stars in a new Moncler campaign—talks with Vogue about her best red-carpet hits, what’s in her winter wardrobe, and if new music is on the way.
body: These days, it’s nothing new to see a brand tap a buzzy A-lister for its new campaign. But for the new “Re/Icons” collection, releasing today, the outerwear label Moncler went all-in on legendary talent—indeed, icons—by enlisting none other than Cher, Grace Jones, and Jennie to model the new winter-ready pieces.

Given that the new drop features reimagined versions of Moncler’s most recognizable styles (including, yes, its signature puffer jackets), it only made sense for such an enduring list of celebrities to wear them. The campaign was shot by Gabriel Moses and features the one and only Cher wearing its sleek Verone puffer jacket in black, as well as the Himalaya jacket in white.

For Cher, the collaboration was a match made in heaven: Turns out, the legendary singer and style icon is a longtime wearer of Moncler’s ski-ready goods. “A long time ago, I had a house in Aspen,” she told Vogue over a phone interview last week. “I would be picking out things to wear, and I liked the simplicity and the cut [of Moncler pieces]. They’re simple but stylish.”
